items.title: China is already at 65.2% EV penetration — Beijing's 2030 target is basically the floor
items.idea: Beijing's new target is 70% of new passenger car sales as NEVs by 2030, but August retail data already put NEV penetration at 65.2%, up ~10 points year-on-year. The real signal isn't NEV growth (total NEV volumes were actually down 10.1% y/y in August) — it's that gasoline car sales collapsed 40% y/y in the same month. Sinopec now sees total Chinese oil demand falling 3.9% in 2026 (~600kbpd), a third straight annual decline, with diesel down 11.4% and gasoline down 8.7%.
items.angle: This is the structural counterweight to every 'China reflation = oil bull' thesis. The ICE car, not the car market, is what's disappearing in China — worth stress-testing any long-China-demand energy position against this.
items.tweetA: China's 2030 EV target is 70% of new car sales. China is already at 65.2% — in August. Gasoline car sales were down 40% y/y while total car sales were down just 10%. The ICE car is what's actually vanishing from China, not the car market. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Everyone models oil demand off Chinese GDP growth. That correlation is breaking: Chinese GDP is up ~20% since 2021, transport fuel demand has barely moved. High oil prices today are funding the EV adoption that kills oil demand tomorrow — permanently, not cyclically.

items.title: IEA just cut 2026 oil demand growth by 1mbpd in a month — while supply fell even faster
items.idea: The September IEA report now sees 2026 global oil demand declining 2.5mbpd, almost 1mbpd weaker than the agency's estimate just a month earlier, as high prices and disrupted supply crush consumption. At the same time global production fell 1.6mbpd in August, observed inventories dropped another 95 million barrels, and crude briefly topped $113/bbl this month — supply is being destroyed faster than demand, which is why the barrel can rally and lose its long-run customer at the same time.
items.angle: This is a violent-unwind setup: near-term supply-driven spike compounding a structural demand shift (see China EV item). Any oil rally built on the Hormuz/supply shock is arguably a shorting opportunity on a 12mo+ horizon, even while near-dated futures stay bid.
items.tweetA: IEA cut 2026 oil demand growth by 1mbpd in a single month — to a 2.5mbpd DECLINE — while global supply fell 1.6mbpd and inventories dropped 95mb in August. Consensus reads that as bullish. It's actually the fastest demand-destruction setup in a decade wearing a supply-shock costume.
items.tweetB: Crude above $113 today is the best sales pitch an EV dealer in Shenzhen could ask for. Every dollar the Hormuz shock adds to gasoline pulls forward Chinese EV adoption that never reverses. This spike is quietly destroying the demand it needs to sustain itself.

items.title: Five unrelated technical signals just started agreeing with each other, right before Fed week
items.idea: This week's chart round-up flags deteriorating market breadth, rising cross-asset correlations, corporate-bond and volatility signals turning cautious, liquidity conditions set to become a headwind, and growth stocks having peaked versus value while semis stagnate — five largely independent technical lenses converging on the same bearish read simultaneously.
items.angle: Breadth, correlation, credit, vol and liquidity rarely all lean the same way at once — when they do, right into a live Fed decision, it's usually the setup for an actual correction rather than just noise. Worth checking VIX term structure and credit spreads for confirmation into Wednesday.
items.tweetA: Five different technical signals — breadth, correlations, credit, vol, liquidity — are all flashing the same warning into Fed week. When indicators that usually contradict each other start agreeing, that's typically when a market actually corrects, not when it just gets nervous.
items.tweetB: Growth has already peaked vs value and semis have gone flat, per this week's chart round-up — before anyone declared a top. If earnings confirm it, the AI-mega-cap-led rally has quietly rotated character while everyone was still watching the index level.

items.title: 14 AI godfathers wrote existential-risk essays since 2024. 12 say a handful should decide. China wrote none.
items.idea: Parekh lays 14 AI-safety essays from US frontier-lab leaders (Pachocki, Amodei x3, Altman, Hassabis, Musk, Sutskever, Bengio, Hinton, Zuckerberg, LeCun) into a matrix by risk named, remedy, timeline and who decides — 12 of 14 assume a small group (labs, regulators, scientists) should control the outcome, every timeline is inside a decade, and only Zuckerberg (distribution to billions) and LeCun (open science) dissent. Zero equivalent essays exist from Chinese lab leaders (DeepSeek, Alibaba Qwen, Moonshot, MiniMax, Z.ai) — China instead named 'loss of control' as a risk from the top via a January 2026 Politburo study session and manages it as compliance (a dedicated but thinly-staffed safety body, boilerplate IPO risk factors) while continuing to ship models.
items.angle: The US policy conversation heading into the September 24 Xi-Trump meeting is being set by essays asking for gates on frontier AI, while China's negotiating posture is chips, memory and open models — not alignment commitments. That asymmetry matters for how export-control and chip-policy headlines should be read this month.
items.tweetA: 14 AI lab leaders have written existential-risk essays since 2024. 12 conclude a handful of people should decide the outcome. Zero of the equivalent Chinese lab leaders have written anything like it — China told its Politburo to treat 'loss of control' as a compliance checkbox and kept shipping models.
items.tweetB: The US walks into the September 24 Xi-Trump meeting with a decade of doom essays setting the agenda. China walks in with chips, memory, and open-weight models. Guess which agenda item has better odds of actually being on the table.

charts.desc: 🔥 CHART WORTH SAVING — the email describes a matrix/table of all 14 essays by risk, remedy, timeline and decision-maker; worth opening for the actual graphic.

items.title: Anthropic's own alignment lead just put a number on human extinction risk — and got 32 million views
items.idea: Anthropic's alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, posted this week that there is 'better than a one-in-ten chance' AI kills every human within a decade, from a lab he says does not yet have a plan for aligning superintelligence — the post drew 32 million views. The same week, per the Wall Street Journal, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the industry over the same concern, comparing it to the Manhattan Project, and Senator Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar filed a bill to ban superintelligence development pending regulation.
items.angle: The company charging for these models just had its own safety lead publish a >10% extinction estimate in the same week Congress moved a bill and a researcher quit outright. Worth watching whether other Anthropic/OpenAI researchers echo the number, and whether it shows up in any AI-regulation-sensitive equity moves.
items.tweetA: Anthropic's own alignment science lead just put a number on it: better than a 1-in-10 chance AI kills every human within a decade — from the company building the models and charging for the privilege. 32 million views and a researcher resignation in the same week isn't marketing, it's a distress signal.
items.tweetB: If the safety lead at the 'responsible' AI lab thinks there's better than a 10% chance of extinction, why is anyone still calling AI regulation premature? Sanders and Casar's bill to pause superintelligence development looks a lot less fringe this week than it did a month ago.

items.title: Goldman's 'buy the AI reset' call is a bet that this hiking cycle is short-lived — and power is the cleanest way to play it
items.idea: With oil near $105/bbl, the US 10-year threatening 5%, and the Fed poised to hike, Goldman's Louis Miller argues the AI trade has already absorbed a meaningful valuation and positioning reset, positioning September's hike as a short cycle rather than the start of a new tightening path. His highest-conviction AI-adjacent trade is power — the cleanest underowned exposure to the physical constraints on the AI buildout — while he flags consumers and housing as the vulnerable spot if $105 oil and a 5% 10-year persist together.
items.angle: This is a specific, falsifiable macro call: Goldman is betting oil-and-rates pain stays contained enough for AI earnings momentum to keep working. Power infrastructure is the position that benefits whether Wednesday's hike is one-and-done or the first of a cycle, since the grid bottleneck thesis doesn't depend on the FOMC path.
items.tweetA: Goldman's read: oil at $105, the 10-year flirting with 5%, the Fed about to hike — and they're calling this the entry point to add AI exposure, not exit it. The whole call rests on 'short-lived hiking cycle.' If Wednesday proves that wrong, this thesis breaks fast.
items.tweetB: Everyone's fighting over whether to own Nvidia or fade it here. Goldman's actual highest-conviction AI trade right now is power — the one part of the stack that works whether the Fed hikes once or five times, because a grid bottleneck doesn't care about FOMC minutes.

items.title: Six weeks ago this Fed decision was a coin flip. Now it's priced above 80% for a hike.
items.idea: August CPI landed close to expectations at the headline (+0.4% m/m, 3.4% y/y) but core ran hot at +0.3% m/m even as the annual core rate ticked down to 2.4% — enough for Fed funds futures to now assign better than 80% odds to a quarter-point hike Wednesday. That repricing has come alongside WTI back near $100/bbl, diesel above $6/gallon, the 10-year briefly testing 5% (only the second time since 2007, after a brief 2023 visit), and the 2-year up roughly 20bp toward 4.6% over the same stretch.
items.angle: The real signal isn't the CPI beat or miss, it's that a hawkish-Fed outcome went from 'razor close' to consensus in six weeks without a single blowout inflation print — oil did more to move this Fed than the data did. Worth flagging as the actual driver behind the recent leg up in yields, not the headline CPI number itself.
items.tweetA: Six weeks ago this FOMC decision was a coin flip. Now Fed funds futures put an 80%+ probability on a hike. The 10-year has only touched 5% twice since 2007 — briefly in 2023, and now. Oil at $100 did more to move this Fed than any data release this quarter.
items.tweetB: Core CPI came in 'only' 0.3% m/m — annualize that and you're back above 3.5% core, not the 2.4% headline everyone's quoting. The Fed isn't hiking because inflation is spiraling; it's hiking because oil made the 'good enough' math turn hot again.

items.title: Wednesday's real question isn't whether the Fed hikes — it's whether it's one hike or the first of a cycle
items.idea: The S&P 500 is up nearly 12% YTD but sits roughly 2% below its mid-August record as the market braces for Wednesday. Fed funds futures already imply an 80%+ probability of a hike, so the actual event risk is whether the statement frames it as a one-off recalibration or the start of renewed tightening — a live test of new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's credibility after his hawkish Jackson Hole speech already moved the curve once, with smaller, debt-financed companies far less able to absorb another leg higher in yields than cash-rich mega-caps.
items.angle: This sets up a dispersion trade independent of the headline hike itself: mega-cap/AI-capex-rich balance sheets vs. small-cap and rate-sensitive names diverge hard depending on Wednesday's language, not on whether the hike itself happens.
items.tweetA: Wednesday isn't 'does the Fed hike' — futures already say yes at 80%+. Wednesday is 'one hike and done' vs 'first of a cycle,' and that's the difference between small caps taking one punch and small caps discovering there are five more rounds on the card.
items.tweetB: Warsh's Jackson Hole speech already moved the curve once. Wednesday is his first live test of whether hawkish talk becomes hawkish policy. Watch the small-cap vs mega-cap spread Wednesday afternoon — a cleaner read on 'cycle vs one-off' than anything in the dot plot.
